title: Vishal Sikka's Hang Ten Systems Raises $53 Million in Second Seed Round
excerpt: The enterprise AI services startup, founded in May by the former Infosys CEO, has now raised $85 million in total after Xora, Temasek's early-stage investment platform, led a $53 million extension closed just five weeks after its first seed round.
body:
• Hang Ten Systems has closed a $53 million seed extension led by Xora, Temasek's early-stage investment platform, bringing its total seed funding to $85 million.
  • The extension closed roughly five weeks after the four-month-old startup's $32 million first seed round, led by Mayfield with participation from Aramco Ventures.
  • Founder and CEO Vishal Sikka, the former Infosys chief executive, says Hang Ten is working with 21 large enterprises as customers or late-stage prospects — including Saudi Aramco, Siemens Energy, and Fresenius Kabi — and has signed multiple seven-figure contracts.
  • The Palo Alto company uses agentic code generation and a reusable skills library to build and modernize enterprise software at a fraction of traditional IT-services cost and time.

Back-to-back seed rounds

Hang Ten Systems, the enterprise AI services startup founded in May by former Infosys chief executive Vishal Sikka, has raised $53 million in a second seed round led by Xora, Temasek's early-stage investment platform. The company told TechCrunch the round closed about five weeks after its initial $32 million seed round, taking total funding to $85 million.

Mayfield, which led the June round, participated again. Other backers include Aramco Ventures, Intel chief executive Lip-Bu Tan, Micron chief executive Sanjay Mehrotra, and Yahoo co-founder Jerry Yang, who sits on the company's board.

The capital follows early traction. Within 25 days of a first meeting with one customer, Hang Ten signed a multimillion-dollar contract to build a mission-critical system — a pace Sikka says he has never seen for enterprise deals. His argument: AI is driving the cost and time of building software toward zero, shifting the work from writing code to defining requirements and validating that systems perform as intended.

"The build part itself has basically become close to zero marginal cost, close to zero time."

— Vishal Sikka, Founder and CEO, Hang Ten Systems

Context and background

Sikka, 59, spent about 12 years at SAP, where he served on the executive board and is credited with creating the HANA in-memory data platform. In 2014 he became the first non-founder chief executive of Infosys, holding the role until 2017. He co-founded the enterprise AI company Vianai Systems in 2019 and left it this April to start Hang Ten.

Hang Ten advises large enterprises — typically with more than $10 billion in annual revenue — on AI strategy, then builds and modernizes their software using agentic code generation, a reusable library of "skills," and a bench of forward-deployed engineers. Its first $32 million round, announced June 24, was led by Mayfield with a strategic investment from Aramco Ventures; early customers included Siemens Gamesa Renewable Energy and Fresenius.

Impact and analysis

The pitch carries some irony: for decades, IT services firms sold labor-heavy customization, integration, and maintenance — the model that made Infosys one of the world's largest IT services companies. Sikka ran that company. Now he is betting AI agents can do much of that work instead, faster and cheaper.

Buyers appear to be responding. Hang Ten says its 21 enterprise customers and late-stage prospects span the United States, Europe, the Middle East, and Asia. Named customers include Saudi Aramco, Siemens Energy — whose wind unit Siemens Gamesa widened its engagement after the startup delivered, per chief executive Vinod Philip — and Fresenius Kabi. Projects so far cover software development, finance analytics, and human resources, according to SiliconANGLE.

"The startup delivered with a quality and speed that genuinely impressed us, and the scope of the work has since been widened."

— Vinod Philip, CEO, Siemens Gamesa

Xora also opens geography: Sikka said the partnership provides an opening into Singapore and Southeast Asia. Xora managing partner and chief investment officer Phil Inagaki said the bottleneck in enterprise AI is implementation — deploying AI "securely, economically and at speed." Aramco Ventures chief executive Mahdi Aladel said the closer his team looks at Hang Ten's approach, "the more functions and use cases we find across our own operations where it would fit," with projects at Aramco already being scoped.

Sikka declined to disclose a valuation but said the extension priced higher than the first round. The incumbents are not standing still: Accenture and Anthropic partnered in 2025 to offer enterprise AI services, and every major consultancy is racing to package agentic delivery of its own.

What's next

The money buys delivery capacity. Hang Ten employs 20 to 25 people across the United States, the Middle East, and Australia, and plans to hire in Europe and India, according to SiliconANGLE. The capital funds current engagements, a bigger engineering and consulting organization, and the platform, infrastructure, and skills library.

The next test is repeatability: converting early, unusually fast wins into a repeatable model across industries is the hurdle between a hot seed-stage story and a genuine challenger to the IT services incumbents — including Sikka's former employer.
nri_angle: The round spotlights a familiar diaspora arc: Vishal Sikka, who once ran Infosys from Bangalore as its first non-founder CEO, is now raising from Singapore's Temasek and Saudi capital in Palo Alto to build the AI-native services firm designed to succeed the labor-arbitrage IT-services model he used to lead.
author: Diaspora Desk
